extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary theorists, and writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply Genette's distinctions and terminology for narrative perspective (focalization), its types, subtypes, tests for identification, and permissible variations/alterations within a narrative. Useful for close reading, narratological analysis, and craft decisions in creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mood (focalization) and voice (narrator identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate the question 'who sees?' (focalization/mood/point of view) with the question 'who speaks?' (narrator/voice). Many theoretical classifications confuse mood and voice by mixing the identity of the narrator with the position of perception that organizes narrative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a narrative, treat focalization (which character's perception organizes the presented information) and voice (who tells the story, authorial intrusions, reliability, etc.) as separate dimensions. Re-evaluate typologies that present these together (e.g., Brooks & Warren, Stanzel, Friedman) and separate modal determinations from narratorial/voicing determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-term typology of focalization (Narrator vs Character relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focalization can be classified by the relation between narrator and character: (1) Narrator > Character (omniscient/vision from behind) — narrator says more than any character knows; (2) Narrator = Character (point of view/restricted field/vision 'with') — narrator says only what a given character knows; (3) Narrator < Character (objective/behaviorist/vision from without) — narrator says less than the character knows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the symbolic formulae (Narrator>Character, Narrator=Character, Narrator<Character) to identify whether the narrative voice provides more, equal, or less information than the character(s). Cite canonical examples (Tom Jones for omniscient, The Ambassadors/What Maisie Knew for internal, Hemingway/Hammett for external) to ground analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: nonfocalized, internal focalization, external focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfocalized narrative = zero focalization (classical omniscient); internal focalization = narrative information is constrained by a character's perspective; external focalization = narrative gives only outward behavior/performance without access to characters' inner thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When labeling sections or works, prefer 'focalization' to 'point of view' to avoid visual connotations. Identify which of the three modes predominates in a passage, noting that the same work can instantiate more than one mode across different sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtypes of internal focalization: fixed, variable, multiple
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal focalization may be (a) fixed — the entire section is through one character (e.g., The Ambassadors, What Maisie Knew); (b) variable — focalizer shifts across sections/episodes (e.g., Madame Bovary switching between Charles and Emma); (c) multiple — several distinct characters each provide focalized accounts of the same events (epistolary novels, The Ring and the Book, Rashomon-style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish these subclasses when analyzing narrative structure. Note that fixed and variable are subclasses of internal focalization; multiple focalization often produces contrapuntal or relativized representations of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict internal focalization criterion (no externalizing of the focal character)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the strict sense, internal focalization requires that the focal character never be described or referred to from the outside, and that the narrator never objectively analyzes that character's thoughts or perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this strict standard to evaluate claims of 'internal' perspective: many supposedly internal passages fail the standard (e.g., Stendhal passages that report Fabrice's inner states in an objective way). Perfect realization occurs in pure interior monologue or works like Robbe-Grillet's La Jalousie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barthes' pragmatic test for internal focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical test for internal focalization: a narrative section belongs to internal focalization if it can be rewritten in the first person without any alteration of the discourse other than changing grammatical pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this transposability test to sentences or passages (e.g., 'Bond saw a man...' can become 'I saw...') to classify focalization; sentences that cannot be so transposed without semantic incongruity (e.g., 'the tinkling of the ice cubes... seemed to awaken in Bond a sudden inspiration') indicate external focalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between narrator's knowledge and focalizer's knowledge (narrator vs focalizer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when narrator and focalizer are the same person (first-person narration), the narrator almost always 'knows' more than the hero did at the moment of the action; thus the narrating function and focalizing function remain distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing first-person narratives, separate the narrator's retrospective knowledge from the focalizer's contemporaneous perceptions. Do not assume oneness of person implies oneness of informational function; consider cases where the narrator deliberately restrains information to reproduce the hero's ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization is sectional and can vary within a work
rubrics_metrics.description: A single focalization formula need not govern an entire work; focalization often applies to definite narrative sections which may be very short. The distinction between points of view can be fluid; what seems nonfocalized can often be analyzed as multifocalized ad libitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse narratives at the level of sections/scenes as well as whole works. Expect transitions, brief alternations, and mixtures of focalization modes; identify where a dominant mode holds and where alterations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alterations: isolated infractions of a dominant focalization code
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations are momentary changes in focalization within a coherent context that function as infractions of the governing code without overturning the overall dominant mode. They take two general forms: giving less information than the code authorizes, or giving more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat isolated focalization shifts as 'alterations' (musical analogy: modulation) rather than necessarily as failures of coherence. Determine whether an apparent inconsistency functions rhetorically (modulation) or disruptively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralipsis (lateral omission) — withholding information
rubrics_metrics.description: Paralipsis is the rhetorical omission of information that in principle ought to be given according to the code of focalization (classical example: withholding an important action/thought that both hero and narrator know but the narrator conceals from the reader until a revelation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify paralipses in detective stories and other genres that depend on withheld information for suspense (Jules Verne, Stendhal, classical detective fiction). Note the effect: reader ignorance preserved intentionally; example: Michel Strogoff concealing a fact the hero knows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralepsis — excess of information (inroad beyond authorized focal field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paralepsis names the opposite alteration: the narrator takes up and gives information that the governing focalization code should leave aside — for instance, intruding into the consciousness of characters other than the focalizer or reporting scenes the focalizer cannot see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize paraleptic passages (e.g., passages in Maisie that report Mrs. Farange's thoughts which Maisie cannot know). Such intrusions can be judged clumsy or purposeful; they constitute excess that must be accounted for in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymodality: person of the narrator does not determine focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The grammatical person or autobiographical nature of the narrator (first- vs third-person, autobiographical narrator) does not mechanically determine focalization: first-person narration does not necessarily equal focalization through the hero, and an autobiographical narrator may freely choose to suppress or reveal later-acquired information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In craft or analysis, do not equate first-person with internal focalization. Consider whether the autobiographical narrator mixes present opinions with past narrative and whether the narrator practices paralipsis by suppressing later knowledge to reproduce a hero's ignorance (Proust, Tristram Shandy, Fielding).

rubrics_metrics.name: External focalization as a technique for mystery and narrative openings
rubrics_metrics.description: External focalization (narrator says less than the character knows) is frequently used to create mystery, to defer revelation, and to present enigmatic openings, especially in the novel of intrigue or adventure (examples: Phileas Fogg, Balzac's openings, Hammett, Hemingway).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing openings or scenes that frame characters as mysterious, identify external focalization as a deliberate technique for withholding interior information and maintaining suspense; note possible reversibility where an external point of view can be reinterpreted as internal via a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and risk of internal focalization in depicting love and subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal focalization is especially effective for portraying the subjectivity of love (e.g., Proust): by adopting the point of view of one protagonist, the author can leave the feelings of the beloved in shadow, producing the 'creature in flight' whose true inner life remains impenetrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal focalization to create narrator/hero-bound ignorance about objects of love; recognize the hermeneutic consequences — many episodes only reveal their full significance later, and some ambiguities (Odette's 'true' feelings) may remain permanently opaque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms of coherence and consistency are not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements such as Lubbock's demand that a novelist be 'consistent on some plan' are debatable; authors (Forster, Booth) have criticized rigid Jamesian rules and defended freedom or strategic inconsistency. Changes of focalization can be legitimate stylistic or rhetorical choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose a blanket norm of uniform focalization; evaluate whether variations serve artistic ends. Distinguish between incoherence that undermines narrative and intentional modulations/alterations that enrich meaning.
